wine.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Grenache and Mourvèdre in roughly equal leading parts, with Syrah, Counoise and smaller parts of the other permitted varieties: the estate grows all thirteen.
wine.sites: One large block around the château at Courthézon, in the north east of the appellation: rolled stones over clay and sand, planted to all thirteen varieties, with much old Mourvèdre.
wine.making: Each variety is picked and fermented apart. The destemmed grapes are first heated briefly and cooled again, the estate's own method, then fermented in vat; the blend is assembled and raised for about a year in large old oak foudres before bottling at the château.
wine.glass: Kirsch and blackberry over leather, game and dried thyme, with black olive, liquorice and a note of truffle as it ages; firm and savoury rather than sweet, the Mourvèdre giving grip and a long, meaty finish.
wine.ageing: Generous on release, it often closes between about five and ten years, then opens again and keeps for two or three decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Burgundy glass.

label.means: The popes' new castle: the cru between Orange and Avignon that permits thirteen named varieties.
The estate at Courthézon, on the north eastern edge of the appellation.

records.table: Château de Beaucastel's Châteauneuf-du-Pape comes from an estate that grows all thirteen permitted varieties, with far more Mourvèdre than most. Savoury rather than sweet, leather, game and kirsch, it can close up in its middle years, so decant it and be patient.
records.story: The name Beaucastel goes back to the sixteenth century, when a family of that name held land at Courthézon. In 1909 the property was bought by an ancestor of the Perrin family, and it has passed down the generations since. Jacques Perrin, who ran it until his death in 1978, set its course: by the family's account he farmed without chemical sprays from the 1950s, and he kept faith with all thirteen of the permitted varieties when many estates grew little but Grenache. Mourvèdre, slow to ripen and hard to grow, became the estate's mark, giving its wine a savoury frame of leather and game, and the brief heating of the harvest before fermentation became its method. When the appellation was founded in 1936 its rules named thirteen grapes, and Beaucastel became the estate that showed what all of them could do together. In 1989 the family first made Hommage à Jacques Perrin, a Mourvèdre led selection kept for strong years, and that same year bought land at Paso Robles with their American importer, the start of Tablas Creek. For a sommelier Beaucastel is the counterweight to Grenache alone, the reason Mourvèdre belongs in any talk of Châteauneuf.

others.name: Hommage à Jacques Perrin

wine.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.sites: Parcels of sand and clay ringed by pine and oak woods in the cool north east of the appellation, many of them facing north, so the Grenache ripens slowly; none of the rolled stones of La Crau.
wine.making: Fermented in vat with little intervention and raised for about a year in old casks and barrels, with no new oak, in the estate's cellar; low yields and late picking do the rest.
wine.glass: Kirsch, raspberry and wild strawberry over incense, rose petal and dried orange peel; pale in the glass, silky and light on its feet for its strength, with fine tannin and a long, perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: Charming within a few years in a ripe vintage, it grows more savoury over fifteen to twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant gently if at all, so as to keep the perfume; a large Burgundy glass.

label.means: The estate's name; on a French label château names a wine estate, here a plain farmhouse in the woods.
The cru between Orange and Avignon, which allows a blend of varieties yet does not require one.

records.table: Château Rayas makes its Châteauneuf-du-Pape from Grenache alone, grown on cool sand among the woods rather than on the famous stones. Pale and perfumed, kirsch, incense and rose, it drinks more like a red Burgundy than a southern blend, so pour it into a Burgundy glass.
records.story: Rayas lies in the woods of the north east of Châteauneuf, on sand rather than stone, and the Reynaud family bought it in 1880. In the next generation the estate began to bottle its own wine and to make its name with Grenache alone, though the rules of the appellation, set down in 1936, allowed thirteen varieties. From 1978 the founder's grandson ran it, a reclusive man with little time for visitors, the press or marketing, who kept a dark cellar of old casks and released his wines when he chose. He died in 1997, and his nephew took charge of Rayas and of the family's Château de Fonsalette in the Côtes du Rhône, keeping the same low yields, late picking and old wood. The estate's fame rests on what it showed: that a Châteauneuf could be pale, perfumed and of one grape, and that cool sand could matter as much as the rolled stones for which the appellation is known. Rayas did this with few words and no fashion. For a sommelier it is the proof that colour and weight are not the measure of a southern red.

wine.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape La Crau
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Grenache, the clear majority, with Mourvèdre and Syrah in smaller parts.
wine.sites: The plateau of La Crau at the eastern edge of the appellation above Bédarrides: a deep bed of rolled quartzite stones, the galets roulés, over red clay that holds water through the summer.
wine.making: Mostly destemmed and fermented in vat, each variety and parcel apart; the blend is then raised in large old oak foudres for well over a year and bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Kirsch and blackberry over dried thyme, lavender and warm stone, with leather and liquorice from the Mourvèdre; full and firm rather than sweet, with fine, dusty tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Generous for a few years after release, it then closes for a while and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The stony plateau of Châteauneuf-du-Pape where the vines grow, not the Crau plain of Provence.
The old telegraph: the optical signal tower that once stood on the plateau.

records.table: Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe's La Crau is Châteauneuf-du-Pape from one stony plateau, where rolled quartzite stones store the day's heat. Grenache led, with Mourvèdre for grip, it tastes of kirsch, thyme and warm stone, and it ages for twenty years.
records.story: The domaine is named for a tower. Claude Chappe (1763 to 1805) devised the optical telegraph in the 1790s, a chain of towers with movable arms that passed messages across France from hilltop to hilltop, and one of them stood on La Crau, the plateau at the eastern edge of what became Châteauneuf-du-Pape. In 1891, by the family's account, a grower of the Brunier family planted vines on the plateau, among stones so thick that the soil beneath them can barely be seen. The holding grew from generation to generation, and when the appellation was drawn in 1936 the plateau lay within it. The galets roulés, quartzite rounded by the ancient Rhône, store the day's heat and give it back at night, while the red clay beneath holds water through the summer, so the old Grenache ripens fully without drying out. The family kept the old name and made La Crau its flagship, with Télégramme, from younger vines, beside it as a second wine. To a sommelier Vieux Télégraphe is the wine to pour when a guest asks what the stones of Châteauneuf actually do.

others.name: Télégramme
others.note: The second wine, Châteauneuf-du-Pape from the domaine's younger vines.

others.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape Blanc
others.note: The white of Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Bourboulenc and Roussanne from the same domaine.

traps: The name comes from an optical telegraph tower on the plateau, not from a vineyard.
La Crau here is a plateau of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, not the Crau plain of Provence.
Télégramme is the second wine, from younger vines, not a lighter style of La Crau.

cards.front: What do the galets roulés of La Crau do for the vines of Vieux Télégraphe?

questions.q: A guest asks why Vieux Télégraphe's La Crau ripens its Grenache so fully. Which reason do you give?

Cool sand under pine and oak woods

questions.exp: The galets roulés of La Crau hold the day's heat and release it at night; cool sand in the woods is Rayas, granite terraces the northern Rhône and limestone crags Gigondas.

wine.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Grenache, the larger part, with an unusually high share of Mourvèdre, some Syrah and small parts of other permitted varieties.
wine.sites: Around two dozen parcels scattered across the appellation, on rolled stones, sand and limestone, blended so that no single soil leads.
wine.making: Destemmed, each variety fermented apart in vat; the blend is then raised in large old oak foudres for a year or more and bottled at the domaine, with no special cuvée drawn off.
wine.glass: Raspberry, kirsch and black cherry over dried thyme, lavender and liquorice, with a savoury edge of leather from the Mourvèdre; fresh and structured for Châteauneuf, with firm, fine tannin.
wine.ageing: Fruity on release, it closes after a few years and opens again towards its tenth year, keeping for two decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a large Burgundy glass.

label.means: The estate's name; the wine is no single walled vineyard but a blend of many parcels.
The cru named for the castle the popes of Avignon built above the village.

records.table: Clos des Papes makes one Châteauneuf-du-Pape red a year, blended from parcels all over the appellation, with more Mourvèdre than most and no special cuvée above it. Fresh and firm, raspberry, thyme and leather, it rewards ten years in the cellar.
records.story: The village takes its name from the popes of Avignon, who built a castle above it in the fourteenth century, and the Avril family, by its own account, has been recorded there since the seventeenth. In 1896, as the family tells it, an Avril bottled wine under the estate name Clos des Papes, when most of the village sold in bulk. In 1923 the growers, led by Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié (1890 to 1967), drew up rules for their wine, on its place, its grapes and its ripeness, that fed into French appellation law, and in 1936 Châteauneuf-du-Pape became an appellation in its own right. Through the twentieth century the family added parcels in every corner of the appellation, until the estate held around two dozen. Where other houses set their old vines apart in prestige cuvées, Clos des Papes kept to one red and one white, and gave the red more Mourvèdre than most, for freshness and structure. That refusal to divide is the estate's signature. For a sommelier it is the example of blending a whole appellation rather than selecting from it, and its white, from six varieties, is a wine to know as well.

others.note: The white, from six varieties in roughly equal parts, a wine that ages for years.

wine.name: Gigondas
wine.classification: A cru of the Rhône Valley, above Côtes du Rhône and its Villages
wine.grapes: Grenache, the greater part, with Syrah, much of it fermented as whole bunches, and a little Mourvèdre.
wine.sites: The estate's parcels around Gigondas under the limestone crags of the Dentelles de Montmirail, on clay and limestone, where height and cool nights keep the wine fresh.
wine.making: Fermented in vat on native yeasts, the Syrah largely as whole bunches; the wine is then raised for about a year in vats, large casks and older barrels before bottling at the estate.
wine.glass: Black cherry and blackberry over smoke, dried thyme and black pepper, with a cool, stony freshness from the limestone; firm but fine tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Open within a few years of the vintage, it is at its fullest between five and fifteen years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant for an hour when young; a large red wine glass.

label.means: A cru under the Dentelles, red and rosé since 1971 and white too from the 2023 vintage.
The family estate's own wine; the house's merchant range, from bought grapes, is labelled Saint Cosme alone.

records.table: Château de Saint Cosme's Gigondas is Grenache, with Syrah fermented as whole bunches, from the foot of the Dentelles, where limestone and cool nights keep it fresh. Black cherry, smoke and pepper, it is a firmer, cooler neighbour to Châteauneuf, made for game or lamb.
records.story: Gigondas lies against the jagged limestone of the Dentelles de Montmirail, and Saint Cosme stands on ground worked since Roman times: vats cut into the rock of its cellars are held to be Gallo-Roman, and a chapel of Saint Cosme gave the estate its name. The Barruol family has held it since 1570. For centuries the wine of Gigondas went out without a name of its own, as Côtes du Rhône and later as Côtes du Rhône Villages, until in 1971 the village became the first of the Villages promoted to a cru, red and rosé, with lower yields and a tighter boundary than its neighbours. In the 1990s a new generation of the family took the estate in hand, began to bottle its lieux-dits apart, Valbelle, Le Claux, Hominis Fides and Le Poste, and set up a merchant business beside it for wines from bought grapes. In 2023 the appellation added white wine to its red and rosé. The estate's Gigondas, the blend of its parcels, is the wine that introduces the house, and the proof that Gigondas is not simply a Châteauneuf from the next valley.
